## Stage1.4 Data Visualisation

library(tidyverse)

# Distribution of violent crime rates
ggplot(data = crime_selected,
       mapping = aes(x = ViolentCrime)) + 
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of violent crime rates",
    x = "Normalised violent crime rate",
    y = "Number of communities"
  )

this histogram shows a positively skewed distribution of normalised violent crime rates. Most communities have relatively low crime rate values, with the highest concentration occurring around 0.05. The frequency decreases as crime values increase. There are also some observations with particularly high crime values near 1. This suggests that there is variation in violent crime rates across communities, which we aim to investigate using socioeconomic variables.

## Stage 3.4 Correlation bar chart 

# Extract correlations with violent crime
crime_correlations <- cor_matrix["ViolentCrime", ]

# Remove violent crime's correlation with itself
crime_correlations <- crime_correlations[
  names(crime_correlations) != "ViolentCrime"
]

# Convert into a data frame
cor_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(crime_correlations),
  Correlation = as.numeric(crime_correlations)
)

# Create bar chart
ggplot(cor_df,
       aes(x = reorder(Variable, -Correlation),
           y = Correlation)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#F28DBB", width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", Correlation)),
    vjust = ifelse(cor_df$Correlation >= 0, -0.5, 1.5),
    size = 4
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-0.6, 0.65)) +
  labs(
    title = "Correlation with Violent Crime",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Pearson Correlation Coefficient"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Poverty (r = 0.52) and unemployment (r = 0.50) have the strongest positive correlations with violent crime, suggesting that communities with higher levels of poverty and unemployment tend to have higher crime rates. On the other hand, median household income (r = -0.42) and education (r = -0.31) have negative correlations, meaning that communities with higher incomes and education levels generally have lower crime rates. Long-term housing vacancy (r = 0.02) shows almost no correlation with violent crime.

Stage4 Modeling Data

4.1 Model Selection

ViolentCrime is a continuous outcome, and this investigation examines how several socioeconomic variables are associated with it simultaneously. So we select Multiple linear regression as the main modelling method. The model will include Poverty, MedianHouseholdIncome, Unemployment, Education and LongTermVacancy. Model fit and residuals will be examined to assess whether this method provides a reasonable summary of the relationships in the data.

4.2 Model Fitting and Results

final_model <- lm(
  ViolentCrime ~ Poverty + MedianHouseholdIncome +
    Unemployment + Education + LongTermVacancy,
  data = crime_selected
)

model_summary <- summary(final_model)

Holding the other variables constant, Poverty (β = 0.429, p < 0.001) and Unemployment (β = 0.245, p < 0.001) were positively associated with violent crime. MedianHouseholdIncome also had a positive coefficient (β = 0.118, p = 0.011). Education (β = −0.145, p < 0.001) and LongTermVacancy (β = −0.171, p < 0.001) had negative coefficients. All five predictors were statistically significant at the 5% level. The income coefficient has a different direction from its bivariate association with violent crime. LongTermVacancy also had a near-zero bivariate correlation but a negative coefficient in the full model. These differences suggest that the adjusted coefficients should be interpreted cautiously. The results describe associations, not causal effects.

4.3 Model Evaluation

model_fit <- data.frame(
  R_squared = model_summary$r.squared,
  Adjusted_R_squared = model_summary$adj.r.squared,
  Residual_SE = model_summary$sigma
)

knitr::kable(
  model_fit,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c("R-squared", "Adjusted R-squared", "Residual standard error"),
  caption = "Model fit"
)
Model fit
R-squared Adjusted R-squared Residual standard error
0.32 0.318 0.192

The model accounted for approximately 32.0% of the variation in violent crime rates (R² = 0.320; adjusted R² = 0.318). This describes how well the model fits the data used in the analysis; it is not a prediction accuracy score for new communities.

 crime_evaluate <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
fit(ViolentCrime ~ Poverty + MedianHouseholdIncome +
    Unemployment + Education + LongTermVacancy,
  data = crime_selected) %>%
  tidy()

The estimate values show us the estimated coefficient of each variable. We can see property, medium household income, and unemployment have a positive relationship to violence crime respectively, if other variables stay constant. However, Education and Long term vacancy do have a negative relationship with violent crime.

Long term vacancy has the lowest value in standard error, it suggests its estimate coefficient is the most precise, it implies that is the most reliable result compared to other variables. Medium household income has the greatest number of standard error, its estimate coefficient is the least compared to other selected variables, its standard value is double the size of long-term vacancy’s.

Statistic is calculated by the formula t = estimate/ standard error, it shows how strong the statistical evidence is, that a regression coefficient is different from zero. Poverty has a large and positive t-value,it gives an evident of poverty has a strong and positive relationship with violent crime. Long term Vacancy is the largest negative coefficient among all the other explanatory variable, as it has the t-value of -7.15

The p-value is used to determine whether there is sufficient statistical evidence, when the p-value is less than 0.05, then it will consider statistically significant. In this report, all the explanatory variable that we have chosen are all less then 0.05, it means they are all statistically significant. Poverty has the smallest p-value, it suggests poverty has a strong statistical evidence against the null hypothesis

residual_data <- data.frame(
  Fitted = fitted(final_model),
  Residuals = residuals(final_model)
)

ggplot(residual_data, aes(x = Fitted, y = Residuals)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, colour = "lightblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "The regression model",
    x = "Fitted violent crime rate",
    y = "Residual"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

The residuals become more spread out at higher fitted values, suggesting that the model errors may be less consistent for communities with higher predicted crime rates. The model should therefore be interpreted with caution in this range.

4.4 Limitations and Possible Improvements

The residual plot suggests that the constant-variance assumption may not hold equally well across the range of fitted values. A future analysis could investigate whether a different model specification improves this pattern. Since the data describe communities rather than individuals, the results should not be used to make claims about individual people or to label particular communities. The analysis identifies associations and does not establish causation.

4.5 predictive Modeling

set.seed(1234)
crime_split <- initial_split(crime_selected)
crime_train <- training(crime_split)
crime_test  <- testing(crime_split)
crime_rec_1 <- recipe(
  ViolentCrime ~ Poverty + MedianHouseholdIncome +
    Unemployment + Education + LongTermVacancy,
  data = crime_selected) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())
crime_mod_1 <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm")
crime_wflow_1 <- workflow() %>%
  add_recipe(crime_rec_1) %>%
  add_model(crime_mod_1)
crime_fit_1 <- fit(crime_wflow_1, data = crime_selected)
crime_predictions_1 <- predict(
  crime_fit_1,
  new_data = crime_test
  ) %>%
  bind_cols(crime_test %>% select(ViolentCrime))
crime_metrics_1 <- crime_predictions_1 %>%
  metrics(truth = ViolentCrime,
          estimate = .pred)
crime_metrics_1

Ethical Concern

In this report, we can see some of the variables have a positive relationship with violent crime. However, the correlation does not imply causation. There are many other factors that can be involved but not take in account. We cannot guarantee the other variables every case in our data is under the same condition. In addition, these data are describing a historical context from 1990, it cannot represent the relationship of violent crime with all those explanatory variables. A huge difference between the 90s and modern day have been made, for example there are changes law, increase in life conditions, compulsory education etc.
